questions.question: A single server can be stopped by an outage, a period in which it cannot work on jobs; a job's net service time is $S_0$. Which description makes the outage non-preemptive?
options: It may start at any moment, and an interrupted job later resumes where it stopped.
It may start only at a service completion, so a started job gets its whole $S_0$ at once.
It may start only when the queue is empty, so no waiting job is ever delayed by it.
Its duration is fixed in advance, so the outage adds no variability to the service.

questions.question: A single server faces four kinds of outage, each with a random duration $R$. Which of them is a preemptive outage in the sense that it can interrupt a job's net service?
options: A setup of random length $R$ carried out before every batch of exactly $B$ jobs
An adjustment that follows a completed job with probability $p$, at an unplanned moment
A failure that can strike while a job is in service, after which the job resumes
A long adjustment between two jobs that delays every job waiting in the queue

questions.question: Non-preemptive outages are added to a single-server queue analysed with Sakasegawa's formula, which uses $\lambda$, $C_a^2$, $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and $C_s^2$. Which of these inputs change?
options: Only $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and $C_s^2$, through the job's effective service time $S$
Only $\lambda$ and $C_a^2$, because outages hold back the flow of jobs into the queue
Only $\mathbb{E}[S]$; $C_s^2$ keeps the value $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)/(\mathbb{E}[S_0])^2$
All four, since $\lambda$ is replaced by the rate at which jobs and outages are completed

questions.question: After each job an adjustment of mean length $\mathbb{E}[R]$ is needed with probability $p$, independently of the job's net service time $S_0$. How does the expected extra time charged to one job depend on $S_0$?
options: It grows in proportion to $S_0$, because a longer job is exposed to outages for longer.
It equals $p\,S_0$, because an adjustment removes a fraction $p$ of the job's service.
It equals $\mathbb{E}[R]$ for every job, because each job can be followed by one adjustment.
It equals $p\,\mathbb{E}[R]$ whatever $S_0$ is, because outages follow job completions.

questions.question: Setups of random length $R$ before every batch of $B$ jobs are compared with adjustments of the same length distribution after each job with probability $p=1/B$, where $B\ge2$ and $\mathbb{E}[R]>0$. How do the effective service times compare?
options: Adjustments have the larger mean $\mathbb{E}[S]$, since random outages come more often.
Mean and variance of $S$ coincide, since outages occur at the same long-run frequency.
The means coincide; adjustments add $p(1-p)(\mathbb{E}[R])^2$ more variance than setups.
The means coincide; setups have the larger variance, since they bundle all outage time.

questions.question: A server needs a setup of mean $\mathbb{E}[R]=4$ hours before every batch of $B=4$ jobs; the net service time has mean $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=1.5$ hours. What is the mean effective service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ of one job?
options: $5.5$ hours
$1.375$ hours
$2.3$ hours
$2.5$ hours

questions.question: After each job an adjustment of mean length $\mathbb{E}[R]=3$ minutes is needed with probability $p=0.2$; the net service time has mean $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=1$ minute. What is the mean effective service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: $1.6$ minutes
$4.0$ minutes
$1.4$ minutes
$3.4$ minutes

questions.question: A server needs a setup before every batch of $B=4$ jobs; $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)=0.75$, $\mathbb{E}[R]=3$ and $\operatorname{Var}(R)=2$ (hours, hours squared), all independent. What is the variance of the effective service time $S$ of one job?
options: $2.75$ hours squared
$1.25$ hours squared
$0.875$ hours squared
$2.9375$ hours squared

questions.question: After each job an adjustment is needed with probability $p=0.25$; its length $R$ has $\mathbb{E}[R]=2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(R)=1$, and $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)=1$ (all independent, in hours). What is $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ of the effective service time?
options: $1.25$ hours squared
$2.25$ hours squared
$2$ hours squared
$2.75$ hours squared

questions.question: Jobs arrive at $\lambda=0.5$ per hour to a stable single server with $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=1$ hour; after each job an adjustment of mean $3$ hours follows with probability $p=0.1$. What long-run fraction of time does the server spend on adjustments?

Adjustments occur after each job with probability $0<p<1$ and have mean $\mathbb{E}[R]>0$. An analyst instead adds the constant $p\,\mathbb{E}[R]$ to every job and uses Sakasegawa's formula with the same $\lambda$ and $C_a^2$. How does the analyst's $\mathbb{E}[W]$ compare?
options: It is the same, because the mean $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and hence the load $\rho$ agree.
It is too low, because $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ loses $p\operatorname{Var}(R)+p(1-p)(\mathbb{E}[R])^2$.
It is too high, because an outage on every job is a heavier load than occasional ones.
It is too low, because the constant model gives a smaller load $\rho$ than adjustments.

questions.question: At a single server, job 1 completes service while jobs 2 and 3 are waiting, and a non-preemptive adjustment of length $R>0$ starts immediately; no other outage occurs. Compared with no adjustment, whose waiting time in the queue increases by $R$?
options: Both job 2 and job 3, since each of them starts its service $R$ later
Only job 1, since $R$ is counted in its effective service time $S$
Only job 2, since the next job absorbs the outage and job 3 is untouched
No job, since the adjustment takes place between jobs, not during service

questions.question: Adjustment indicators $F$ satisfy $\mathbb{P}(F=1)=p$ but are more likely after long jobs, so $F$ and $S_0$ are positively correlated; $R$, with $\mathbb{E}[R]>0$, is independent of $(S_0,F)$. For $S=S_0+FR$, which of the formulas $\mathbb{E}[S]=\mathbb{E}[S_0]+p\mathbb{E}[R]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=\operatorname{Var}(S_0)+p\operatorname{Var}(R)+p(1-p)(\mathbb{E}[R])^2$ still holds?
options: Both still hold, since only the overall adjustment probability $p$ enters them.
Neither holds, since an outage linked to job length makes the outage preemptive.
Only the mean formula holds; $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ gains $2\operatorname{Cov}(S_0,FR)>0$.
Only the variance formula holds; the mean needs $p$ conditional on a long job.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at $\lambda=0.5$ per hour at a single server with $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=1.6$ hours, and a setup of mean $\mathbb{E}[R]=4$ hours precedes every batch of $B$ jobs. What is the smallest integer $B$ for which the queue is stable?

A server needs a setup before every batch of $B=4$ jobs; $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)=0.5$, $\mathbb{E}[R]=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(R)=2$ (hours, hours squared), all independent. What is the SCV $C_s^2$ of the effective service time?

Adjustments of mean $1.5$ hours follow a job with probability $p=0.2$. Alternatively, failures strike during service at rate $\lambda_f=0.1$ per hour of service, with repairs of mean $1.5$ hours. For which net service time $S_0$ is the expected extra time per job equal?
options: $S_0=2$ hours
$S_0=0.5$ hours
$S_0=3$ hours
$S_0=0.3$ hours

questions.question: A single server serves jobs $1,2,3,\dots$ in this order; all of them are present from the start, and job $j$ needs net service time $S_{0,j}$. Exactly one outage of length $R>0$ occurs. In case I it is non-preemptive and starts the moment job $2$ completes; in case II it is preemptive and strikes in the middle of job $2$, which resumes afterwards. How do the two cases compare?
options: Every job from job $3$ onwards departs $R$ earlier in case I, because there the outage is not part of any job's service time.
The total busy time of the server is larger by $R$ in case II, because job $2$ then occupies it for $S_{0,2}+R$ instead of $S_{0,2}$.
Job $2$ departs $R$ later in case II; all other departure times and the total busy time are the same in both cases.
All departure times coincide in the two cases, because the same outage of length $R$ occurs exactly once in both and all jobs are present.

questions.question: Setups of length $R$ before every batch of $B$ jobs, independent of the net service times, are added to a single server whose net service time has $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)>0$. Compared with $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)/(\mathbb{E}[S_0])^2$, what happens to the SCV $C_s^2$ of the effective service time?
options: It always rises, because $\operatorname{Var}(S)\ge\operatorname{Var}(S_0)$ for every setup.
It can fall, since $\mathbb{E}[S]$ grows too, e.g. a fixed $R$ with very variable $S_0$.
It can rise or fall, but only through $\operatorname{Var}(R)$: a fixed $R$ leaves $C_s^2$ unchanged.
It always falls, because spreading $R$ over $B$ jobs averages its variability out.

questions.question: Poisson arrivals ($\lambda=0.5$ per hour, $C_a^2=1$) reach one server with $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=1.2$ hours; outages with one length distribution of mean $4$ hours come as setups every $B=10$ jobs or as adjustments with $p=0.1$. By how much is Sakasegawa's $\mathbb{E}[W]$ larger for adjustments?
options: $0$ hours
$3.6$ hours
$2.0$ hours
$1.8$ hours

questions.question: Poisson arrivals ($\lambda=0.6$ per hour, $C_a^2=1$) reach one server with $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=1.5$ hours and $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)=0.45$; a fixed setup of $3$ hours precedes every batch of $B=10$ jobs. What are the load $\rho$ and the long-run mean waiting time $\mathbb{E}[W]$ according to Sakasegawa's formula?
options: $\rho=1.08$, so $\mathbb{E}[W]$ has no finite value
$\rho=0.9$ and $\mathbb{E}[W]\approx8.1$ hours
$\rho=0.9$ and $\mathbb{E}[W]\approx9.2$ hours
$\rho=2.7$, so $\mathbb{E}[W]$ has no finite value
